Issued at 446 PM CDT Tue Aug 18 2026

-- FORECAST CHANGES OF NOTE/BIG PICTURE COMMENTS:
- No truly "notable" forecast changes worth discussing in
  detail, as we remain in a seasonably-warm and active weather
  pattern with various/intermittent rain/thunderstorm chances
  due to our region residing along the large-scale interface 
  between large-scale upper high pressure/riding centered to our
  south- to-southwest...and broad troughing/low pressure 
  centered to our north-to-northeast. 

- In the "minor details" department, high temps have trended up
  slightly (at least a few degrees) for days such as Wednesday,
  Thursday and Monday as our tendency lately has been for highs
  to end up a bit warmer than forecasts from a few-to-several
  days out have called for. 


-- 7-DAY FORECAST CHRONOLOGICAL RUNDOWN (through Tues. Aug. 25):
- CURRENT/RECENT WEATHER SCENE AS OF 345 PM:
In the wake of convection within mainly the northeast half of
our CWA Monday evening into early this morning that admittedly
"overachieved" in intensity and areal coverage (significant 
wind damage/some hail damage in Ord area from intense supercell 
pre- midnight...a more widespread area of damaging winds post- 
midnight and even flooding rains in limited areas), fortunately 
the bulk of today (and especially this afternoon) has been 
"quiet/dry...as we reside "in between upper level 
disturbances/shortwave troughs (the next one approaching from WY
per water vapor satellite/short term model data/analysis). At 
the surface, winds have trended to a mainly light (under 10 MPH)
and variable direction regime. 


- THIS EVENING-OVERNIGHT:
While MOST areas will remain dry/thunderstorm-free through at
least 9-10 PM (except for some spotty sprinkles/light showers
here or there), anytime after that is "fair game" for the
development of more widespread (at least scattered)
showers/thunderstorms as the aforementioned upper wave arrives
from the northwest and sparks at least (mainly) slighly-elevated
storms. Convective instability (CAPE) does not appear as high as
last night, but deep-layer shear will remain seasonably-strong
(at least 40-50KT), so at least a few strong to severe storms
appear possible. Admittedly, higher-res models runs (such as
from HRRR) from 24 hours ago did not verify well for last night,
but again leaning on the latest consensus of HRRR/NAMNest, the
first round of overnight convection should mainly focus into the
southern half of our CWA, as convection rolls in from the west
off the High Plains, while other storms developing along the
low-level frontal zone/along the exit region of the low level
jet (LLJ) MIGHT flirt with our eastern KS zones
(Jewell/Mitchell), but SHOULD mainly affect areas near the KS/NE
border slightly east of our CWA. Then, very late in the night
(mainly 4-7 AM), high-res models are hinting at a secondary area
of strong/severe storms developing into our northern CWA (north
of I-80) out of northern NE. 

Low temps tonight mainly 60s, as breezes remain fairly light 
but mainly trend more northerly. 


- WEDNESDAY DAYTIME-EVENING (pre-midnight):
Honestly, our potentially biggest (and obviously first) concern
could be right away in the morning mainly 7-10 AM, as the
aforementioned potential cluster of strong/severe storms in our
northern CWA rides into our eastern counties (somewhat similar
to this morning, albeit later in the morning). Whether or not
this unfolds, from mid-morning onward through late afternoon
MOST of our CWA should remain dry as the upper wave passes by
(similar to today). That being said, very intentionally left at
least slight chances (20%) for spotty convection going for the
majority of the CWA through the entire day and into the evening,
in case any convection redevelops on the backside of departing
activity, and/or spotty new (and potentially supercellular)
development occurs during peak heating. Fortunately, high-res
models show any late afternoon-evening severe storm potential
being VERY isolated in the wake of departing upper forcing, but
cannot argue with SPC maintaining a broad Marginal Risk...just
in case. 

Otherwise during the day Wednesday, high temps were nudged up
slightly, but this still looks like the overall-coolest day of
the next week most areas...ranging upper 70s-low 80s north...to
mid-upper 80s in KS and Furnas County area. Breezes mainly under
10 MPH and northerly to easterly. 


- WEDNESDAY LATE NIGHT (post-midnight):
Fortunately, we should (in theory) catch a break from any late-
night/early AM convection for a change, as most models are
outright-dry and our official forecast follows suit. Depending
on sky cover/clearing trends, this could be a night to watch for
fog potential. Low temps mainly low-60s (one of our coolest
nights upcoming). 


- THURSDAY-THURS NIGHT: 
The daytime looks mainly dry, but the late afternoon into the
overnight carries at least small rain/thunderstorm chances
arrive with the next subtle disturbance dropping in from the
